plan.contextChunk: This figure shows two fragments of a recursion tree side by side, labeled (a) and (b), with nodes carrying subproblem sizes. In (a) a top node labeled n has two branches: the left ends at a bare 0 with no box drawn around it, the right at a node labeled n-1. A large pale gray ellipse encloses the top node and the n-1 node together, and a heavy dotted arrow runs from that ellipse rightward to the expression Theta(n). The n-1 node branches in turn to two gray rectangles reading (n-1)/2 - 1 and (n-1)/2. In (b) a single node labeled n is ringed by a small pale gray ellipse, again with a dotted arrow pointing right to Theta(n), and it branches to two gray rectangles that both read (n-1)/2. The shared Theta(n) tag is the point of the comparison: the shaded groupings cost the same in each panel, while the boxed subproblems still waiting differ. Putting a lopsided split followed by an even one beside a single even split motivates the argument that alternating bad and good partitions costs about what uninterrupted good partitioning would.

interactionPlan.concept: A bad (maximally unbalanced) partition immediately followed by a good one costs Θ(n) for the pair and leaves subproblems of essentially the same size as a single good partition — so alternating bad and good splits still gives O(n lg n).

interactions.label: Replay construction (optional)
interactions.teaches: How each panel's tree is built one partition at a time, so the learner sees that panel (a) spends two partitions and panel (b) one to reach the same subproblem sizes.
interactions.notes: Default state 'complete figure' must render the entire two-panel source figure exactly as described in elements; the other states are a purely optional progressive-disclosure replay.

interactions.label: Focus
interactions.teaches: That isolating either fragment reveals the same Θ(n) charge and the same ≈(n−1)/2 leftover subproblems.
interactions.notes: Focusing does not delete the other panel's geometry in the default view; it dims it.

interactions.teaches: Which partitioning work is bundled into the single Θ(n) charge: clicking an ellipse brightens it and the node labels it encloses, and clicking a gray box highlights the matching-size box in the other panel.

demo_steps.title: The figure as printed
demo_steps.narration: Both fragments are shown complete: (a) a bad split into 0 and n−1 followed by an even split, and (b) a single even split. Each shaded region is charged Θ(n).

demo_steps.title: Start from the same subproblem
demo_steps.narration: Optional replay: strip both panels back to their roots. Each begins with an identical subproblem of size n and no cost charged yet.

demo_steps.title: A worst-case split in (a)
demo_steps.narration: Panel (a)'s first partition is maximally unbalanced: it peels off an empty side (0) and leaves n−1. It still costs Θ(n) but makes almost no progress.

demo_steps.title: A good split absorbs it
demo_steps.narration: The n−1 subproblem splits evenly into (n−1)/2 − 1 and (n−1)/2. The tilted ellipse groups the bad and good partitions together — their combined cost is still only Θ(n).

demo_steps.title: One balanced split alone
demo_steps.narration: Panel (b) spends a single Θ(n) partition and produces two subproblems of size (n−1)/2 — the same sizes, to within one element, as panel (a) ended with.

demo_steps.title: Same cost, same remaining work
demo_steps.narration: Back to the full figure: both fragments charged Θ(n) and both left ≈(n−1)/2-sized subproblems. The bad split cost only a constant factor, not extra depth.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: A bad split absorbed into the next good split costs the same Θ(n) and leaves the same subproblem sizes as one good split alone — so alternating bad and good partitions changes only the constant, not the O(n lg n) running time.

Progressive disclosure is optional and only reached via demo steps. Use a wide viewbox matching the source's landscape proportions (roughly 2:1 width to height) with node and box text sized large (~26–30 units) so labels read comfortably at inline size. Panel (a) on the left, panel (b) on the right, generous whitespace between. Nodes are plain italic serif math text with no circles; edges are thin straight black lines. Panel (a): 'n' near the top, a short edge down-left to a bare unboxed '0' set low and left, a longer edge down-right to 'n−1'; a large light-gray filled ellipse tilted about 45° hugs the n→n−1 edge enclosing both labels; a thick black dotted arrow leaves its right side and points to 'Θ(n)' in larger serif type. Below 'n−1', two short edges lead to light-gray filled rectangles whose centered text reads '(n−1)/2 − 1' (left, wider box) and '(n−1)/2' (right) — every rectangle must contain its text, none may be blank. Panel (b): a single 'n' inside a small light-gray ellipse, the same thick dotted arrow to 'Θ(n)' at the same vertical height, and two long edges splaying to two equal light-gray rectangles both reading '(n−1)/2', set wider apart than in (a). Italic '(a)' and '(b)' centered beneath each fragment. Do NOT draw a third recursion level, grandchildren boxes, legends, or running-cost captions. Highlighting brightens an ellipse fill to pale amber and its enclosed labels; states earlier than 'complete figure' simply omit the not-yet-drawn elements rather than graying them.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Toggle between the alternating bad-good split and the balanced split: the shaded Theta(n) cost group stays comparable while the remaining subproblem boxes change, making clear why the two fragments can have similar level cost.
- Button for expanding the next recursion level: each press reveals the children produced by the current split and updates the accumulated cost label, making clear how partition balance controls the shape of the recursion tree.
- Click for a shaded ellipse: the nodes included in that Theta(n) grouping brighten together, making clear which partitioning work is being counted as one level of cost.

authoredContext:
In the average case, PARTITION produces a mix of “good” and “bad” splits. In a recursion tree for an average-case execution of PARTITION, the good and bad splits are distributed randomly throughout the tree. Suppose, for the sake of intuition, that the good and bad splits alternate levels in the tree, and that the good splits are best-case splits and the bad splits are worst-case splits. Figure 7.5(a) shows the splits at two consecutive levels in the recursion tree. At the root of the tree, the cost is n for partitioning, and the subarrays produced have sizes n 1 and 0: the worst case. At the next level, the subarray of size n 1 undergoes best-case partitioning into subarrays of size .n 1/=2 1 and .n 1/=2. Let’s assume that the boundary-condition cost is 1 for the subarray of size 0. The combination of the bad split followed by the good split produces three subarrays of sizes 0, .n  1/=2  1, and .n  1/=2 at a combined partitioning cost
of ‚.n/ C ‚.n  1/ D ‚.n/. Certainly, this situation is no worse than that in
Figure 7.5(b), namely a single level of partitioning that produces two subarrays of
size .n  1/=2, at a cost of ‚.n/. Yet this latter situation is balanced! Intuitively,
the ‚.n  1/ cost of the bad split can be absorbed into the ‚.n/ cost of the good
split, and the resulting split is good. Thus, the running time of quicksort, when levels alternate between good and bad splits, is like the running time for good splits
alone: still O.n lg n/, but with a slightly larger constant hidden by the O-notation.
We shall give a rigorous analysis of the expected running time of a randomized
version of quicksort in Section 7.4.2.

interactions.label: Partition pattern
interactions.teaches: That the shaded Θ(n) work and the resulting subproblem sizes in the alternating case are essentially identical to those of a single balanced partition.

interactions.label: Expand next recursion level
interactions.teaches: How each partition step generates children and adds Θ(size) work, so partition balance directly controls the shape and depth of the recursion tree.
Which nodes' partitioning work is bundled together into the single Θ(n) charge for that level.

demo_steps.title: Two roots of size n
demo_steps.narration: Both fragments start from the same subproblem of size n. Nothing has been partitioned yet, so no children exist and no cost has been charged.

demo_steps.title: A worst-case split in (a)
demo_steps.narration: In panel (a) the first partition is maximally unbalanced: it peels off an empty side (0) and leaves n−1. That partition still costs Θ(n), but makes almost no progress.

demo_steps.title: A good split follows
demo_steps.narration: The n−1 subproblem is then partitioned evenly into (n−1)/2 − 1 and (n−1)/2. The shaded ellipse groups the bad and good partitions together — their combined cost is still only Θ(n).

demo_steps.title: One balanced split alone
demo_steps.narration: Panel (b) spends a single Θ(n) partition and produces two subproblems of size (n−1)/2 — the same sizes, to within one element, as panel (a) ended with.

demo_steps.title: Same cost, same remaining work
demo_steps.narration: Side by side: both fragments charged Θ(n) and both left roughly (n−1)/2-sized subproblems. The bad split cost only a constant factor, not an extra level of depth.

demo_steps.title: Continuing downward
demo_steps.narration: Expanding one more level shows both trees marching toward the same depth, which is why alternating bad and good partitions still runs in O(n lg n).

plan.keyInsight: A bad split absorbed into the next good split costs the same Θ(n) as one good split alone — so alternating bad and good partitions only changes the constant, not the O(n lg n) running time.

Italic serif labels '(a)' and '(b)' centered beneath each fragment. discrepancies: Panel labels "(a)" and "(b)" are rendered in italic in the generated figure, whereas the source shows them upright in regular roman type.

The dotted Θ(n) arrows are noticeably thinner and their dots finer than the source's heavy, chunky dotted arrows with the distinctive bar-and-triangle head; at inline scale they read as faint dotted lines rather than bold pointers.

Overall drawing is scaled down inside a 1000×300 viewbox within a taller container, leaving a large empty band below the figure and making all mathematical labels smaller than the source implies relative to the canvas.
In panel (a) the tilted ellipse is proportionally narrower than the source's, so the 'n' label sits nearly on its boundary rather than comfortably inside the shaded region as in the original.

Source panel (a) shows the two gray boxes at slightly different sizes/heights (the left box wider and lower); generated boxes are aligned on a common baseline with equal height, a minor layout difference.

plan.concept: A bad (maximally unbalanced) partition immediately followed by a good one costs Θ(n) for the pair and leaves subproblems of essentially the same size as a single good partition — so alternating bad and good splits still gives O(n lg n).

interactions.label: Replay construction (optional)

interactions.label: Focus

interactions.teaches: Which partitioning work is bundled into the single Θ(n) charge: clicking an ellipse brightens it and the node labels it encloses, and clicking a gray box highlights the matching-size box in the other panel.

demo_steps.title: The figure as printed
demo_steps.narration: Both fragments are shown complete: (a) a bad split into 0 and n−1 followed by an even split, and (b) a single even split. Each shaded region is charged Θ(n).

demo_steps.title: Start from the same subproblem
demo_steps.narration: Optional replay: strip both panels back to their roots. Each begins with an identical subproblem of size n and no cost charged yet.

demo_steps.title: A worst-case split in (a)
demo_steps.narration: Panel (a)'s first partition is maximally unbalanced: it peels off an empty side (0) and leaves n−1. It still costs Θ(n) but makes almost no progress.

demo_steps.title: A good split absorbs it
demo_steps.narration: The n−1 subproblem splits evenly into (n−1)/2 − 1 and (n−1)/2. The tilted ellipse groups the bad and good partitions together — their combined cost is still only Θ(n).

demo_steps.title: One balanced split alone
demo_steps.narration: Panel (b) spends a single Θ(n) partition and produces two subproblems of size (n−1)/2 — the same sizes, to within one element, as panel (a) ended with.

demo_steps.title: Same cost, same remaining work
demo_steps.narration: Back to the full figure: both fragments charged Θ(n) and both left ≈(n−1)/2-sized subproblems. The bad split cost only a constant factor, not extra depth.

plan.keyInsight: A bad split absorbed into the next good split costs the same Θ(n) and leaves the same subproblem sizes as one good split alone — so alternating bad and good partitions changes only the constant, not the O(n lg n) running time.
plan.reconstructionNotes: IMPORTANT: the default/initial render is the complete two-panel source figure — both panels fully drawn with ellipses, all edges, both labeled gray boxes each, the dotted arrow and Θ(n). Progressive disclosure is optional and only reached via demo steps. Use a wide viewbox matching the source's landscape proportions (roughly 2:1 width to height) with node and box text sized large (~26–30 units) so labels read comfortably at inline size. Panel (a) on the left, panel (b) on the right, generous whitespace between. Nodes are plain italic serif math text with no circles; edges are thin straight black lines. Panel (a): 'n' near the top, a short edge down-left to a bare unboxed '0' set low and left, a longer edge down-right to 'n−1'; a large light-gray filled ellipse tilted about 45° hugs the n→n−1 edge enclosing both labels; a thick black dotted arrow leaves its right side and points to 'Θ(n)' in larger serif type. Below 'n−1', two short edges lead to light-gray filled rectangles whose centered text reads '(n−1)/2 − 1' (left, wider box) and '(n−1)/2' (right) — every rectangle must contain its text, none may be blank. Panel (b): a single 'n' inside a small light-gray ellipse, the same thick dotted arrow to 'Θ(n)' at the same vertical height, and two long edges splaying to two equal light-gray rectangles both reading '(n−1)/2', set wider apart than in (a). Italic '(a)' and '(b)' centered beneath each fragment. Do NOT draw a third recursion level, grandchildren boxes, legends, or running-cost captions. Highlighting brightens an ellipse fill to pale amber and its enclosed labels; states earlier than 'complete figure' simply omit the not-yet-drawn elements rather than graying them.
